title: Classes and Objects
summary: Write your own class with private fields, a constructor, methods and toString, create objects with new, and understand references, encapsulation and static members.
introduction: So far every program was one class with static methods. Real Java programs model the things they deal with, accounts, orders, players, as classes: a class bundles data (fields) with the operations allowed on that data (methods), and each object created from it carries its own state. In this lesson you write a BankAccount class, create accounts with new, protect the balance behind methods, learn why two variables can point at one object, and see what static really means.
learningObjectives: Declare a class with fields, a constructor and methods, and create objects with new
Hide state behind private fields and expose behaviour through public methods
Explain how object references behave when assigned or compared
Use static fields and methods for data shared by all objects

blocks.text: A bank account has an owner and a balance, and a few things may happen to it: deposits, withdrawals, statements. Scattering those as loose variables and methods works for one account and falls apart for a thousand. A **class** describes the data and the behaviour once; an **object** (also called an instance) is one concrete account created from that description with `new`. The class is the blueprint, the objects are the houses, and every house has its own rooms.

Put the class in its own file, `BankAccount.java`. **Fields** hold the state of each object. The **constructor** has the class name and no return type; it runs when `new` creates an object and sets the fields. Inside the class, `this` refers to the object the method was called on, which is needed when a parameter has the same name as a field. The **methods** are the only way code outside the class can change the balance.

blocks.title: BankAccount.java

blocks.text: A second file holds the program that uses the class. Since Java 22 the source launcher compiles both files when you run `java Main.java` in that folder; with `javac` you would compile both: `javac Main.java BankAccount.java`.

blocks.text: `new BankAccount("Ada", 100)` allocates an object, runs the constructor, and returns a reference that is stored in `account`. The dot calls a method on that particular object, so `account.deposit(50)` changes this account's balance and nobody else's. `System.out.println(account)` calls `toString` automatically; without your own `toString` Java prints the class name, an `@` and a hexadecimal hash code, which is rarely what you want.

The fields are `private`, so `account.balance = 1000000;` does not compile outside the class. Every change goes through `deposit` and `withdraw`, which is where the rules live: no negative deposits, no overdrafts. This is **encapsulation**: hide the data, expose behaviour. Add a getter such as `getBalance` only when other code genuinely needs to read the value, and add a setter only when free changes are really allowed. Here `owner` is also `final`, so it is set once in the constructor and never changes.

A variable of a class type does not hold the object; it holds a **reference** to it. Assigning one variable to another copies the reference, so both names point at the same object and a change through one is visible through the other. `==` compares references, which is why two separately created accounts with identical data are not `==`. A reference that points at nothing holds `null`, and calling a method on `null` throws a `NullPointerException`.

blocks.title: Inside main

blocks.text: A `static` field belongs to the class, not to any object: there is exactly one copy, shared by every instance. A `static` method likewise runs without an object and is called on the class name. Use static for counters, caches and utility methods such as `Math.max`, and for constants declared `static final`. `main` is static precisely because no object exists yet when the program starts.

blocks.title: Ticket.java

blocks.text: A static method cannot use `this` or touch instance fields, because there is no particular object to read them from; `error: non-static variable number cannot be referenced from a static context` is the message when you try.

Fields you do not initialise get a default value, unlike local variables, which must be assigned before use. Relying on defaults is fine for counters that start at zero; for references, remember that the default is `null`.

blocks.title: The parameter that shadows the field
blocks.text: In a constructor `BankAccount(String owner) { owner = owner; }` compiles without complaint but does nothing: both names refer to the parameter, and the field stays `null`. Write `this.owner = owner;` whenever a parameter and a field share a name. A `NullPointerException` from a field you were sure you had set is the usual symptom.

blocks.title: One class, one file, one job
blocks.text: Keep each public class in its own file named after it, and keep the class focused: an account knows about money, not about printing reports or talking to databases. Small classes with clear responsibilities are the heart of readable Java; the [Object-Oriented Programming](/tutorials/object-oriented-programming) tutorial goes deeper into design.

questions.question: What is the value of an `int` field that no constructor or method has assigned?
questions.explanation: Fields get default values: numeric types are 0, booleans are false and references are null. Only local variables must be assigned explicitly before use.

questions.question: `BankAccount b = a;` creates a second, independent copy of the account object.
questions.explanation: The assignment copies the reference, not the object. Both variables point at the same account, and a deposit through `b` is visible through `a`.
